questions.question: Which of the following products is NOT covered by the microbial enumeration method described in USP <61>?

options.A: A product containing live microorganisms as an active ingredient, such as a live-bacteria preparation
options.B: A non-sterile drug substance expected to contain mesophilic aerobic bacteria and fungi
options.C: A preparation whose compliance must be judged against an established microbiological quality specification
options.D: A non-sterile preparation with antimicrobial activity that must be neutralized before testing

questions.explanation: <61> is used to quantitatively enumerate mesophilic bacteria and fungi that can grow under aerobic conditions, in order to determine whether a substance or preparation meets a microbiological quality specification. It states explicitly, however, that the method is not applicable to products whose active ingredient is a live microorganism. Products with antimicrobial activity remain testable once that activity is removed or neutralized.

questions.question: Which statement about the positioning of the most-probable-number (MPN) method in <61> is correct?

options.A: The MPN method has the highest precision and is therefore the preferred method for all types of products
options.B: The MPN method and membrane filtration have comparable precision and may be interchanged freely according to each laboratory's habits
options.C: The MPN method is suitable only for enumerating molds, because its results for molds are the most reliable and stable
options.D: It is generally the least accurate method, but may be the most appropriate for some products with an extremely low bioburden

questions.explanation: <61> states that the MPN method is generally the least accurate method for enumeration, but that it may be the most appropriate method for certain product groups with a very low bioburden. MPN is especially unreliable for molds, so it is not the method of choice for mold enumeration.
questions.reference: USP <61> Microbial Enumeration Tests › Enumeration Methods

questions.question: A laboratory subcultured a test strain for 7 consecutive passages from the original master seed-lot and then used it directly for inoculation. Under <61>, what is the status of this practice?

options.A: It does not comply; the strain must not be more than five passages removed from the original master seed-lot
options.B: It complies, as long as the same lot of medium is used for every passage, so the number of passages is unlimited
options.C: It does not comply; the strain must be purchased anew from a commercial source each time, and seed-lots may not be used
options.D: It complies, as long as the final inoculum is kept to no more than 100 cfu, so the number of passages is unrestricted

questions.explanation: <61> requires a seed-lot system so that the viable microorganisms used for inoculation are not more than five passages removed from the original master seed-lot. Seven passages exceeds this. An inoculum of no more than 100 cfu is a separate requirement and cannot offset the limit on passages.
questions.reference: USP <61> Microbial Enumeration Tests › Growth Promotion Test, Suitability of the Counting Method and Negative Controls › Preparation of Test Strains

questions.question: The product being tested has antimicrobial activity, and the analyst added an inactivator and a surfactant during sample preparation. Under the general procedures of <61>, what must be demonstrated?

options.A: That the inactivator and surfactant have both been sterilized and are present in the product at a concentration below 1%
options.B: That the inactivator has a sufficient shelf life and that a certificate of analysis from the supplier has been obtained
options.C: That the inactivator is efficacious and non-toxic, and that the surfactant is non-toxic and compatible with the inactivator
options.D: That the inactivator is effective only against the test strains and can completely degrade the antimicrobial components in the product

questions.explanation: <61> specifies that if an inactivator is used, its efficacy and its non-toxicity to microorganisms must be demonstrated; if a surfactant is used, it must be shown to be non-toxic to microorganisms and compatible with the inactivator used. The conditions listed in the other options do not appear in the original text.
questions.reference: USP <61> Microbial Enumeration Tests › General Procedures

questions.question: During a <61> test, a negative control using the chosen diluent in place of the test sample shows microbial growth. How should this be handled?

options.A: Treat it as a normal background value and subtract the negative control colony count from the sample count before interpreting
options.B: The negative control has failed and an investigation is required, because there must be no microbial growth in the negative control
options.C: Repeat the test with a higher concentration of neutralizer, without recording or investigating the cause of the failure
options.D: As long as the sample count is below the acceptance criterion, the negative control result need not be considered in the validity of the test

questions.explanation: The negative control confirms the test conditions: the diluent is used in place of the test preparation, and the result must show no microbial growth. A negative control must also be run alongside product testing. A failed negative control must be investigated and cannot simply be subtracted or ignored.
questions.reference: USP <61> Microbial Enumeration Tests › Growth Promotion Test, Suitability of the Counting Method and Negative Controls › Negative Control

questions.question: In growth promotion testing of media, what is the maximum acceptable difference between the count obtained on solid medium and the calculated value for the standardized inoculum?

options.A: It must not differ by more than a factor of 10, because colony variability on solid media is large
options.B: It must not differ by more than a factor of 5, because the inoculum is capped at 100 cfu
options.C: It must not differ by more than a factor of 2, because this is the acceptance criterion for solid media
options.D: It must not differ by more than a factor of 1.5, because it must almost exactly match the standardized inoculum

questions.explanation: The count recovered on solid medium must not differ from the calculated value of the standardized inoculum by more than a factor of 2. For liquid media, clearly visible growth comparable to that obtained with a previously approved batch is required.
questions.reference: USP <61> Microbial Enumeration Tests › Growth Promotion of the Media

questions.question: In suitability testing, when the microbial suspension is added to the prepared sample dilution, what is the limit on the inoculum volume?

options.A: No more than 1% of the volume of the diluted product, and no more than 100 cfu in the inoculum
options.B: No more than 10% of the volume of the diluted product, and no more than 1000 cfu in the inoculum
options.C: No less than 1% of the volume of the diluted product, and at least 100 cfu in the inoculum
options.D: No more than 5% of the volume of the diluted product, and no more than 500 cfu in the inoculum

questions.explanation: The inoculum volume should not exceed 1% of the volume of the diluted product, and the inoculum should not exceed 100 cfu, so that adding a large volume of suspension does not dilute the product or alter the test conditions. The proportions and counts in the other options are not the values in the original text.
questions.reference: USP <61> Microbial Enumeration Tests › Suitability of the Counting Method in the Presence of Product › Inoculation and Dilution

questions.question: In suitability testing, the count recovered in the product group is 5 times lower than in the control group (inhibition of more than a factor of 2). Which of the following is an appropriate modification listed in <61>?

options.A: Raise the inoculum above 100 cfu to offset the inhibitory effect of the product on the microorganisms
options.B: Shorten the incubation time so the inhibitory effect does not have time to fully manifest over the incubation period
options.C: Use a lower incubation temperature so that the activity of the antimicrobial components in the product is weakened
options.D: Switch to membrane filtration, add a neutralizing agent, or increase the volume of diluent or medium

questions.explanation: A recovery reduced by more than a factor of 2 indicates inhibition of growth, so the procedure must be modified. The approaches listed in the original text include increasing the volume of diluent or culture medium, adding specific or general neutralizing agents, membrane filtration, or a combination of these. Raising the inoculum, shortening the incubation time, or changing the incubation temperature are not approaches listed in the text and cannot demonstrate acceptable recovery.
questions.reference: USP <61> Microbial Enumeration Tests › Suitability of the Counting Method in the Presence of Product › Neutralization/Removal of Antimicrobial Activity

questions.question: According to Table 2, if the interfering substance is EDTA (edetate), what is the listed potential neutralizing agent?

options.A: Lecithin, the same neutralizer used for quaternary ammonium compounds and parabens
options.B: Magnesium or calcium ions, used to counteract the chelating action of EDTA
options.C: Thiosulfate, the same neutralizer used for mercurials and halogens
options.D: Glycine, the same neutralizer used for aldehyde interfering substances

questions.explanation: In Table 2, the neutralizing agent corresponding to EDTA is magnesium or calcium ions. Lecithin corresponds to QACs, parabens, and the like; thiosulfate corresponds to mercurials, halogens, and aldehydes; and glycine corresponds to aldehydes. None of these is a neutralizer for EDTA.
questions.reference: USP <61> Microbial Enumeration Tests › Neutralizing Agents, Table 2

questions.question: In suitability testing using the MPN method, three consecutive 10-fold dilutions are prepared and three portions of each dilution are inoculated into tubes of Soybean-Casein Digest Broth. How many tubes are inoculated in total?

options.A: 3 tubes, because only one representative tube per dilution is needed
options.B: 6 tubes, because the MPN is usually calculated from the results of two dilutions
options.C: 9 tubes: three tubes for each of the three dilutions, incubated for not more than 3 days
options.D: 12 tubes: three tubes for each of the three dilutions, plus three negative control tubes

questions.explanation: The MPN method requires preparing at least three consecutive 10-fold dilutions, and three portions of 1 g or 1 mL from each dilution are inoculated into three tubes containing 9 to 10 mL of SCDB, giving 9 tubes for the three dilutions. They are incubated at 30° to 35° for not more than 3 days, and the MPN is then read from Table 3.
questions.reference: USP <61> Microbial Enumeration Tests › Recovery of Microorganisms in the Presence of Product › Most-Probable-Number (MPN) Method

questions.question: Unless otherwise specified, what is the standard sample amount for product testing under <61>?

options.A: 10 g or 10 mL of product; 10 containers for aerosols and 10 patches for transdermal patches
options.B: 1 g or 1 mL of product; 1 container for aerosols and 1 patch for transdermal patches
options.C: 100 g or 100 mL of product; 20 containers for aerosols and 20 patches for transdermal patches
options.D: 10 g or 10 mL of product; 20 containers for aerosols and 5 patches for transdermal patches

questions.explanation: Unless otherwise specified, use 10 g or 10 mL of the product; for liquids or solids in aerosol form, sample 10 containers; for transdermal patches, sample 10 patches. The amounts and numbers of units in the other options are not those specified in the original text.
questions.reference: USP <61> Microbial Enumeration Tests › Testing of Products › Amount Used for the Test

questions.question: When enumerating a product by membrane filtration or the pour-plate method, what are the incubation conditions for the two media?

options.A: SCDA at 20° to 25° for 5 to 7 days; SDA at 30° to 35° for 3 to 5 days
options.B: Both SCDA and SDA at 30° to 35° for 3 to 5 days
options.C: Both SCDA and SDA at 20° to 25° for 5 to 7 days
options.D: SCDA at 30° to 35° for 3 to 5 days; SDA at 20° to 25° for 5 to 7 days

questions.explanation: Soybean-Casein Digest Agar for enumerating TAMC is incubated at 30° to 35° for 3 to 5 days, and Sabouraud Dextrose Agar for enumerating TYMC is incubated at 20° to 25° for 5 to 7 days. The option that swaps the two temperatures is a common mix-up.
questions.reference: USP <61> Microbial Enumeration Tests › Testing of Products › Examination of the Product › Plate-Count Methods

questions.question: In the pour-plate method, the plate from a given dilution with the highest number of colonies, but below what number, should be used to calculate cfu?
questions.explanation: Select the plate corresponding to a dilution that has the highest number of colonies but fewer than 250 for TAMC and fewer than 50 for TYMC, take the arithmetic mean for each medium, and convert to cfu per g or per mL of product. The option "TAMC below 50, TYMC below 250" swaps the two values.
questions.reference: USP <61> Microbial Enumeration Tests › Testing of Products › Examination of the Product › Plate-Count Methods › Pour-Plate Method

questions.question: When both bacterial and mold colonies grow on an SCDA plate, how should TAMC be interpreted? Also, what can be done when the TYMC is expected to exceed the criterion because of bacterial growth?

options.A: Count only bacterial colonies, excluding molds; repeat the incubation using SCDA with an antifungal agent added
options.B: Record bacteria and molds separately and do not include them in TAMC; use a lower incubation temperature
options.C: All colonies on SCDA count toward TAMC, including molds; SDA containing antibiotics may be used
options.D: Count only mold colonies, excluding bacteria; use SDA and extend the incubation to 14 days

questions.explanation: TAMC equals the total cfu on SCDA, and any fungal colonies present are also counted; TYMC equals the cfu on SDA, and any bacterial colonies present are likewise counted. When the TYMC is expected to exceed the acceptance criterion because of bacterial growth, SDA containing antibiotics can be used.
questions.reference: USP <61> Microbial Enumeration Tests › Testing of Products › Interpretation of the Results

questions.topic: Reduced sample size for small batches
questions.question: A clinical trial preparation batch consists of only 150 units in total. Under <61>, to what number can the sample size for this batch be reduced at most?

options.A: 2 units, because for batches of fewer than 200 it may be reduced to two units
options.B: 1 unit, because for batches of fewer than 200 it may be reduced to one unit
options.C: 10 units, because the sample size is not adjusted for batch size
options.D: 5 units, because for batches between 100 and 200 half is taken

questions.explanation: When the total number of items in a batch is less than 200 (for example, clinical trial samples), the number of samples can be reduced to two units; if it is less than 100, it can be reduced to one unit. A batch of 150 falls between 100 and 200, so two units apply.
questions.reference: USP <61> Microbial Enumeration Tests › Testing of Products › Amount Used for the Test
